problem: The trap says Borůvka may add an edge whose two ends are already in one component. Borůvka only ever chooses an edge leaving a component, so an internal edge is never a candidate; the real risk is that two different components choose the same edge, which must be added once, not twice.
fix: In Borůvka an edge joins two different components by construction; the mistake to guard against is counting the same chosen edge twice when two components pick it, which would make a cycle. Add each distinct chosen edge once, then relabel the merged components.

problem: The rule 'keep only the smaller vertex's choice' never says what the larger vertex does, so the student cannot see how the root appears.
fix: In a two-vertex cycle u↔v with u < v, u keeps pointing to v and v drops its pointer and points to itself, so v becomes the root of that tree.

where: Section 1 formula box and Quiz Q7
problem: The O(n²) per-round cost with an adjacency matrix holds only for the round that scans rows to find each vertex's cheapest neighbour. Pointer-jumping rounds touch only the parent array and cost O(n) whatever the storage, so 'work per round = O(n²)' and 'a matrix round scans n² cells' overstate every round.
fix: Say: the hooking round costs O(n²) with an adjacency matrix and O(n + m) with an adjacency list; each later pointer-jumping round costs O(n) with either storage (the matrix version is quoted as O(n²) only as a loose upper bound).

where: Section 2, paragraph on Prim and Kruskal
problem: 'Their parallel versions ... still need a global order' is not right for Prim. Parallel Prim keeps a priority queue of frontier edges and grows one tree; it does not need the edges in a single sorted global order the way Kruskal does.
fix: Kruskal needs the edges in one global sorted order and adds one edge at a time; parallel Prim instead grows a tree from a root and needs a shared priority queue of frontier edges. Borůvka avoids both because every component chooses independently.
